World.summary: In a WhatsApp exchange Mandelson told Starmer’s chief of staff at the time, Morgan McSweeney, to ‘solve your Darren issue’ – referring to Darren Jones The Liberal Democrats are saying the UK needs a proper plan for immigration. This is from the party’s asylum and immigration spokesperson, Paul Kohler . Britain needs to regain control of its immigration system after the chaos of Brexit. Yet sixteen years after David Cameron’s ‘tens of thousands’ pledge, six prime ministers and ten home secretaries have overseen wild swings in immigration numbers with net migration now set to fall below zero. Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services. The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level. British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour’s high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high. British families are left to pay for it with lower wages, longer waits for a GP appointment and homes they cannot afford. Mass low-skilled immigration must end completely as it is bad for our economy and corrosive to our society. Continue reading...

Business.summary: We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford. If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people. The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. Culture.title: Lumière album review – finding solace in the rich, lyrical world of French cello music
Culture.summary: Laura van der Heijden/Jâms Coleman (Chandos) The piano-cello duo explore the consoling beauty of works by Franck, Fauré and Mel Bonis, with a welcome rediscovery among the highlights This is the third release from the team of cellist Laura van der Heijden and pianist Jâms Coleman . They say it grew from a desire to record “music of consolation and warmth”, and every piece on this all-French programme fits the bill. The most substantial is Franck’s 1886 Sonata, best known in its original, violin-and-piano version but also claimed by cellists ever since the composer sanctioned an arrangement not long after its premiere. It gets a persuasively expansive performance here. Coleman’s piano is unfailingly clear and detailed; van der Heijden’s playing is angry and urgent in the second movement, impassioned in the climactic passages of the finale. More generally, though, her melodies spool out in endless lines, her tone rich and sustained, her phrasing unbroken almost to a fault: just occasionally the cello line feels as if it could use more breath, more space in which to ask questions. There’s a sense of security in that sustained tone, though, and it serves the consolatory aspect of the programme well. Massenet’s Méditation from Thaïs and Fauré’s bittersweet Sicilienne are the most familiar of the shorter pieces; alongside these there are a transcription of Paix, a melancholy yet consolatory song by Charlotte Sohy; the compact and characterful Three Pieces by Nadia Boulanger; and a characteristically lovely Élégie by the still-underrated Darius Milhaud. And from Franck’s protege Mel Bonis we hear the 1904 Cello Sonata, a searching work that manages to feel tautly argued and rhapsodic at the same time – a worthwhile rediscovery. Continue reading...

Culture.title: Bob Dylan review – at 85, he is in finer voice now than he was 40 years ago
Culture.summary: Bournemouth International Centre Kicking off yet another UK leg of his Never Ending Tour, Dylan may seem to treat his audience with indifference – but his songs are given imaginative, probing arrangements Norman Mailer once asked whether a reader would finish The Old Man and the Sea if they did not already know Ernest Hemingway was the author. There are moments during this Bob Dylan set – the first of another UK leg of his so-called Never Ending Tour – where I wonder what we would make of tonight’s music if we were not aware of the identity of the now 85-year-old performer. Ever since beginning the Never Ending Tour in the late 80s, Dylan has disdained crowd pleasing platitudes, preferring to reinterpret his vast oeuvre in his inimitable “late style”: the subdued jazz version of Tangled Up in Blue dropped halfway through the show is typical of his tendency to insulate old material in a new arrangement. Dylan’s decision to kick off these dates in Bournemouth at a time of year when the town’s wealthy snowbirds will have headed farther south, exhibits the same wilfulness, as does the very way he performs on stage. One can imagine Dylan rattling through tonight’s set even if the BIC were empty, a scenario completely congruous with his apparent indifference to the audience hellbent on deciphering his every syllable.
